title: Introducing Sarvam Token Factory
gist: A provider in India launched its serving stack for its own and open models. An orchestrator agent reads fleet telemetry and hands experiments to sub-agents per layer; a simulator calibrated on its servers filters candidates before live A/B tests, and an engineer approves each change. The post lists eight changes tested on one model, six kept, and bugs it found in an upstream fused kernel.
changes: Another provider runs the loop in production, and the first to say a simulator screens changes before live tests. Its gains sit where the build order says: cache tier, prefill and routing, with first-token time 2.1x better than the stock stack on the same nodes. An upstream fused kernel had shipped a correctness bug.
caveats: All numbers are its own. The 1.9x throughput figure compares with a public board's published run, not a rerun on its hardware, and that run had speculation off at the top load. The agent loop gets one paragraph: no count of agent-found changes, no cost, and nothing on how well the simulator predicts. Whether its kernel fixes went upstream is not stated.

bears_on.note: An upstream fused kernel shipped without a clamp and garbled about one long code reply in nine. Its own changes pass a simulator, a live test and an engineer.
A private stack returns the first token 2.1x sooner than the stock open one on the same nodes, and reports 1.9x a public board's throughput.
Agents run dozens of experiments per model in days, with a person approving each change.
It says each new model breaks kernel, cache and scheduling assumptions that must be fixed within hours of release.
